q: In the sentence "The young cadet answered confidently," the word "confidently" is a:
expl: It modifies the verb "answered" and tells how the action was performed.

q: Which word is a pronoun in "They completed the obstacle course"?
expl: "They" stands in place of a noun.

q: In "Honesty is essential for leadership," the word "Honesty" is a:
expl: It names an abstract quality.

q: Which word is an adjective in "She gave a brief answer"?
expl: "Brief" describes the noun "answer".

q: In "The candidates waited outside," "outside" functions as a:
expl: It tells where they waited.

q: Which of the following is a conjunction?
expl: "Because" joins clauses and introduces a reason.

q: In "The book is on the desk," "on" is a:
expl: It shows the relationship between "book" and "desk".
An interjection expresses sudden feeling or emotion.

q: In "Ali and Hamza trained together," "and" is a:
expl: It joins two coordinate nouns.

q: Which word is a common noun?
expl: "River" names a class, not a unique proper name.

q: In "He can swim well," "can" is a:
expl: "Can" is a modal auxiliary expressing ability.

q: Which option contains a possessive pronoun?
expl: "Mine" stands alone as a possessive pronoun; "my" is a possessive determiner.

q: In "The wounded soldier recovered," "wounded" is functioning as a:
expl: It describes the noun "soldier".

q: The word "but" in "He was tired but continued" is a:
expl: "But" is a coordinating conjunction showing contrast.
The -ing form names an activity and serves as the subject.

q: Which sentence contains an adverb of frequency?
expl: "Often" tells how frequently the action occurs.

q: In "This is the man who helped us," "who" is a:
expl: It introduces a relative clause and refers to "man".

q: Which word is a determiner/article in "An officer entered the room"?
expl: "An" is the indefinite article modifying "officer".
It intensifies the adjective "careful".

q: Which pair consists entirely of prepositions?
expl: Both "in" and "on" express relationships of place/time.

q: Choose the correct form: "He ___ to the academy every morning."
expl: A habitual action with a third-person singular subject takes "goes".

q: "They ___ the task before the instructor arrived."
expl: Past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions.
"Since Monday" with an ongoing action calls for present perfect continuous.

q: "At 8 p.m. yesterday, we ___ for the test."
expl: An action in progress at a specific past time uses past continuous.
Future perfect shows completion before a future point.
"Trained" with a finished past time is simple past.

q: "The bus ___ before we reached the stop."
expl: The bus departure happened before another past event.
"Listen!" signals an action happening now.

q: "She ___ in Rawalpindi for five years." (She still lives there.)
expl: Present perfect links a past beginning to the present.

q: "When I was a child, I ___ cricket every evening."
expl: A completed past habit takes simple past.

q: "This time tomorrow, we ___ the written test."
expl: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a future time.

q: Which sentence is in present perfect tense?
expl: Present perfect uses have/has + past participle.

q: "If he studies hard, he ___ the test."
expl: First conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb.

q: "He ___ for two hours before the rain stopped."
expl: Past perfect continuous emphasizes duration before another past event.
Universal truths normally use simple present.
A longer background action interrupted in the past uses past continuous.
Present perfect is has + past participle.

q: "By the time you arrive, I ___ the report."
expl: Completion before a future arrival takes future perfect.
Stative verb "know" is normally not used in the continuous form.
A definite finished time "last week" requires simple past.

q: Choose the correct article: "He is ___ honest man."
expl: "Honest" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent.
"Engineer" begins with a vowel sound.
Unique objects such as the sun normally take "the".
"University" begins with the consonant sound /ju:/.
Names of rivers take the definite article.
Sports generally take no article when used generically.

q: "She is ___ best candidate in the group."
expl: Superlatives normally take "the".
"One" begins with a /w/ consonant sound.
"Hour" begins with a vowel sound because h is silent.
Plural mountain ranges take "the".

q: Which phrase normally takes no article?
expl: Individual mountain peaks normally do not take an article.

q: "He went to ___ school to attend his class."
expl: Institutional use of "school" for its primary purpose often takes no article.

q: "His father went to ___ school to meet the principal."
expl: Here the school is a specific building/institution, not merely the activity of schooling.
"Umbrella" begins with a vowel sound; "raincoat" with a consonant sound.

q: "___ Quran is the holy book of Islam."
expl: Names of well-known sacred texts are conventionally used with "the" in this construction.
"European" begins with /j/, a consonant sound.
Names of continents normally take no article.
The letter M is pronounced /em/, beginning with a vowel sound.

q: "This is ___ same book that I borrowed."
expl: "The same" is the standard expression.
Names of languages normally take no article.
The standard collocation is "good at".
The standard collocation is "interested in".
Use "at" for exact clock times.
Use "on" for days and dates.
Use "in" for years.
"Across" expresses movement from one side to the other.
"Since" marks the starting point of an action continuing to the present.
"For" expresses a duration.
"Between" is standard for two distinct parties.
"Among" is used for a group of more than two.
The standard collocation is "accused of".
"Belong to" is the correct construction.
The standard collocation is "afraid of".
"Above" indicates a higher position.
"Beside" means next to; "besides" means in addition to.
